ety.text: From Middle English don, from Old English dōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, do, make”). For senses 4 and 5, compare Old Norse duga, also Northern English dow. The past tense form is from Middle English didde, dude, from Old English dyde, *diede, an unexpected development from Proto-Germanic *dedǭ/*dedē (the expected reflex would be *ded), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰédʰeh₁ti, an athematic e-reduplicated verb of the same root *dʰeh₁-.

Coined by Italian musicologist Giovanni Battista Doni in 1635 as an easier-to-sing open-syllable revision to the solmization ut of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin Dominus (“The Lord”) (speculated by some to be an ulterior abbreviation of Giovanni Battista Doni) on the pattern of other Latinate solfège with the stated justification that God is the tonic and root of the world.
Shortening of dozen.

senses.d: A syntactic marker in a question whose main verb is not another auxiliary verb or be.
ex: Do you go there often?

senses.d: A syntactic marker in negations with the indicative and imperative moods.
ex: I do not go there often.
Do not listen to him.

senses.d: A syntactic marker for emphasis with the indicative, imperative, and subjunctive moods.
ex: But I do go sometimes.
Do tell us.

senses.d: A syntactic marker that refers back to an earlier verb and allows the speaker to avoid repeating the verb; in most dialects, not used with auxiliaries such as be, though it can be in AAVE.
ex: I play tennis; she does too.
Likes her cappuccino, Mary does. (UK, colloquial)

senses.d: Should; ought to (especially in respect of a task to be repeated).
ex: Do I just call every number on the list each time?

senses.d: Used to form the present progressive of verbs.
ex: ...An' the dogs do bark, an' the rooks be a-vled to the elems high and dark, an' the water do roar at mill.
